paras: The threatened lynching of George Nickel took place at Brownsville, Pennsylvania, in August 1881, when neighbors of Dr. George Nickel threatened to lynch him for alleged cruelty to his young wife. Nickel left the town for "parts unknown" and was not harmed, and the episode survives only as a one-sentence item in Pennsylvania news columns.

Nickel, a doctor, was described as living at Brownsville in what the item called Washington county. His neighbors accused him of cruelty to his "young wife" and threatened to lynch him, though the item gives no details of the alleged cruelty, the neighbors' number or any gathering. To escape what the item called "the wrath of his neighbors," Nickel left for "parts unknown." Neither copy names his wife or states the race of anyone involved.
No report of a complaint, arrest or court case against Nickel, or of any action against the neighbors, appears in the coverage.

The earliest copy appeared on August 19, 1881, in the Cambria Freeman of Ebensburg, buried among unrelated paragraphs in its "News and Other Notings" column. A day later the Carbon Advocate of Lehighton printed the same sentence, word for word, under "State News." Both papers ran it without comment or headline, as one of many brief items of state and national news. The identical wording suggests both drew on a single unnamed source, and no local Brownsville account was found.

bases: Neighbors threatened to lynch Nickel for alleged cruelty to his wife and he fled; no violence followed, and neither brief states anyone's race (A1, A2).

No one was killed: the briefs report only a threat by "his neighbors" to lynch Nickel, who fled (A1, A2). The threat was extralegal and rested on an accusation of cruelty to his wife, but the number of neighbors is not given.
The two briefs are word-for-word the same state-news item, so they are reprints of one unnamed source, not independent reports (A1, A2).
